q:
Federal agents execute a search warrant at Donnelly’s apartment, which the government contends is the hub of an illegal sports-betting business. During the two-hour search, the apartment’s landline rings eleven times. Agent Ruiz answers each call. Each caller, unprompted, says something like “Put two hundred on the Eagles, minus three” or “Give me the over on the Sixers.” None of the callers is identified.

At Donnelly’s trial for operating an illegal gambling business, the government calls Agent Ruiz to recount the calls to prove that the apartment was being used to accept bets. Donnelly objects on hearsay grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because the callers’ words are offered to prove their belief that bets could be placed at the apartment, and that belief is probative only if it is accurate.
Sustain the objection unless the government produces at least one caller for cross-examination, because the sincerity of anonymous declarants cannot otherwise be tested.

Overrule the objection, because the callers did not intend to assert that the apartment was a betting establishment, so their utterances are not offered to prove the truth of any matter they asserted.
Overrule the objection, because each call is a present sense impression describing the caller’s own conduct while he was engaged in it.
Overrule the objection, but only if the court finds the callers unavailable, because each caller’s attempt to place an illegal bet was a statement against penal interest.
e: Rule: A “statement” is a person’s oral or written assertion, or nonverbal conduct the person intended as an assertion. FRE 801(a). Hearsay is a statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted in it. FRE 801(c). Under the Federal Rules, the declarant’s intent controls: words or conduct not intended to assert the fact they are offered to prove are not hearsay, even when they reveal the declarant’s belief in that fact.
oe: This is the common-law reasoning of Wright v. Doe d. Tatham, which treated implied assertions as hearsay. The Federal Rules rejected that approach by defining “statement” by reference to the declarant’s intent to assert.
Nothing in the hearsay rule requires producing a declarant whose words are not hearsay. Anonymity can bear on weight or Rule 403, but it does not turn non-hearsay into hearsay.
Correct. The callers did not intend to assert that the apartment was a betting operation, so their utterances are not hearsay when offered to prove it.
A present sense impression must describe or explain an event or condition. A betting instruction describes nothing, and no exception is needed for words that are not hearsay in the first place.
Rule 804(b)(3) requires unavailability and, in a criminal case, corroborating circumstances. More basically, it presupposes hearsay. The calls are not hearsay, so the exception is beside the point.
topic: Definition & non-truth uses — FRE 801(a) · FRE 801(c)

q:
Paloma sues Ridgeline Freight, Inc. and its former driver, Hatch, for injuries suffered when a Ridgeline tractor-trailer that Hatch was driving on Ridgeline business ran a red light and struck her car. Ridgeline fired Hatch the morning after the crash. That afternoon, a newspaper reporter visited Hatch at home, and Hatch said: “Look, it was on me. I was texting dispatch and never saw the light change.”

Hatch and Ridgeline are tried together. Paloma calls the reporter to repeat Hatch’s statement. Both defendants object.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit it against both defendants, because the statement concerned a matter, the operation of the truck, that was within the scope of Hatch’s employment.
Admit it against both defendants as a statement against interest, because it exposed Hatch to civil liability.
Exclude it entirely, because by the time Hatch spoke he had been fired, so the statement could not have been against his interest when made.
Exclude it as to Hatch, because a party’s statement is admissible only if made on personal knowledge, and a driver who “never saw” the light change cannot know when it changed.
Admit it against Hatch only and, on request, instruct the jury not to consider it against Ridgeline.
e: Rule: A party’s own statement is not hearsay when offered against that party. FRE 801(d)(2)(A). A statement by a party’s agent or employee is attributable to the party only if it concerns a matter within the scope of the relationship and was made “while it existed.” FRE 801(d)(2)(D). When evidence is admissible against one party but not another, the court must, on timely request, restrict it to its proper scope. FRE 105.
oe: The scope-of-employment element is satisfied, but the timing element is not. Rule 801(d)(2)(D) requires the statement to be made while the employment relationship existed, and Hatch had already been fired.

Rule 804(b)(3) applies only if the declarant is unavailable. Hatch is a party sitting in the courtroom. And an against-interest statement would not be binding on Ridgeline as an admission in any event.
Opposing-party statements need not be against interest when made. That requirement belongs to Rule 804(b)(3). The termination matters only to whether the statement can be attributed to Ridgeline.
The advisory committee notes free party admissions from the firsthand-knowledge requirement. Hatch also had knowledge of what matters most here: he knew he was texting and not watching the light.
Correct. The statement is Hatch’s own admission, but it cannot be attributed to Ridgeline because it was made after the employment ended.
topic: Opposing-party statements — FRE 801(d)(2)(A) · FRE 801(d)(2)(D)

q:
At 4:12 p.m., a motorist calls 911 and, in an even, unhurried voice, says: “There’s a red Silverado, plate JKT-4471, that just passed me on I-95 northbound doing probably a hundred, weaving across all three lanes. I’m at mile marker 12.” The caller gives no name and hangs up.

At 4:21 p.m., a red Silverado with that plate crosses the median near mile marker 19 and kills another driver. In the estate’s wrongful-death suit against the Silverado’s driver, the estate offers the 911 recording, properly authenticated, to prove that the Silverado was speeding and weaving. The caller has never been located.

Is the recording admissible?
o: No, because the caller’s calm demeanor shows that he was not under the stress of excitement caused by a startling event.
Yes, as a present sense impression, because the caller described the truck’s driving while or immediately after perceiving it.
Yes, but only if the estate shows that it could not locate the caller despite reasonable efforts.
No, because an unidentified declarant’s personal knowledge cannot be established.
No, because a call made to a government 911 operator is testimonial.
e: Rule: A present sense impression is a statement describing or explaining an event or condition, made while or immediately after the declarant perceived it. FRE 803(1). Unlike an excited utterance, it requires no startling event and no excitement; its reliability comes from contemporaneity, which leaves no time for calculated misstatement. Rule 803 exceptions apply whether or not the declarant is available.
oe: Calm demeanor would hurt an excited-utterance argument under 803(2), but 803(1) has no excitement requirement.
Correct. The statement describes an event while or immediately after the declarant perceived it.
Availability is immaterial under Rule 803. Unavailability matters only for the Rule 804 exceptions.
Personal knowledge can be inferred from the content and circumstances of the statement. Courts scrutinize anonymous declarants carefully, but anonymity is not a per se bar.
The Confrontation Clause applies only in criminal prosecutions. Even in a criminal case, a 911 call reporting an ongoing danger is typically nontestimonial under Davis v. Washington.
topic: 803: spontaneity, state of mind, medical — FRE 803(1) · FRE 602

q:
After an intersection collision, Officer Breen arrives within minutes. Her report, prepared under a department regulation requiring officers to document every collision, states: (1) “Measured 62 feet of skid marks behind Vehicle 2”; and (2) “Witness Lena Ortiz, a pedestrian, stated: ‘The blue car (Vehicle 2) ran the red.’” Breen did not record when Ortiz made the statement or her demeanor. Ortiz cannot be located.

In the civil suit by the driver of Vehicle 1 against the driver of Vehicle 2, the plaintiff offers a certified copy of the report without calling Officer Breen. The defendant objects to the entire report.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the entire report, because Officer Breen had a legal duty to record accurately what witnesses told her.
Exclude the entire report, because Rule 803(8) excludes matters observed by law-enforcement personnel.
Exclude the entire report, because a public record is admissible only through the testimony of its author or custodian.
Admit the skid-mark measurement, but exclude Ortiz’s statement unless it independently satisfies a hearsay exception.
Admit the entire report as a business record, because the police department regularly prepares such reports.
e: Rule: A public record setting out a matter observed while under a legal duty to report is admissible, except that in a criminal case it may not include matters observed by law-enforcement personnel. FRE 803(8)(A)(ii). When a record contains a statement by someone who had no duty to report, that inner statement is a second layer of hearsay and must satisfy its own exception. FRE 805; Johnson v. Lutz. A certified copy of a public record is self-authenticating. FRE 902(4).
oe: Breen’s duty extends to her own observations, not to the truth of what a bystander told her. The informant must also be acting under a duty for the inner statement to ride along; that is the lesson of Johnson v. Lutz.
The law-enforcement exclusion in 803(8)(A)(ii) applies only in criminal cases. This is a civil suit.
Public records can be authenticated by certification under Rule 902(4). No live witness is required.
Correct. The officer’s observation is admissible under 803(8)(A)(ii). The bystander’s statement is a separate layer that needs its own exception under Rule 805.

Rule 803(6) has the same limitation: a statement by an outsider who is not part of the business’s regular reporting chain is not covered. Johnson v. Lutz was itself a police-report case under the business-records statute.
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 803(8)(A)(ii) · FRE 805

q:
A federal grand jury investigating a bid-rigging cartel subpoenas Vance, a cement contractor. Under a grant of immunity, Vance testifies that Corrigan never attended any cartel meeting. The prosecutors already believed Vance was lying but did not confront him, because they did not want to reveal their wiretap evidence while the investigation was ongoing.

Corrigan is later indicted. At trial, Vance, who now faces perjury exposure, invokes the Fifth Amendment, and the court sustains the privilege. Corrigan offers the transcript of Vance’s grand jury testimony. The government objects.

What is the court’s proper approach?
o: Admit the testimony only if it finds that the government had a similar motive to develop Vance’s testimony at the grand jury as it would at trial, an inquiry to which the government’s reasons for not confronting Vance are relevant.
Admit the testimony, because the government chose to call Vance before the grand jury and, as a matter of adversarial fairness, cannot now avoid testimony it elicited.
Exclude the testimony, because a grand jury proceeding is not a “trial, hearing, or lawful deposition.”
Exclude the testimony, because a declarant who invokes a privilege is not “unavailable” when the government has the power to immunize him again.
Admit the testimony, because statements made under oath and under a grant of immunity carry sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness.
e: Rule: Former testimony of an unavailable declarant is admissible if, in a criminal case, it is offered against a party who had an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross, or redirect examination. FRE 804(b)(1). A witness who properly invokes a privilege is unavailable. FRE 804(a)(1).
oe: Correct. This is the Salerno and DiNapoli framework: no adversarial-fairness shortcut, and a fact-specific similar-motive inquiry.
The Supreme Court rejected this adversarial-fairness argument in Salerno. The text of 804(b)(1) requires similar motive with no exception.
Courts treat grand jury testimony as testimony given at a hearing for purposes of 804(b)(1). The fight is over motive, not the type of proceeding.
A sustained privilege claim makes the declarant unavailable under 804(a)(1). The government’s refusal to immunize again does not change that.
Oath and immunity bear on reliability, but 804(b)(1) turns on similar motive, not general trustworthiness. That argument belongs under Rule 807, which has its own requirements.
topic: 804: declarant unavailable — FRE 804(b)(1) · FRE 804(a)(1)

q:
Police respond to a report of a domestic disturbance at the Voss home. They find Lena Voss alone on the front porch, appearing “somewhat frightened” but saying nothing is wrong. Inside, they see a shattered glass space heater. One officer keeps Curtis Voss in the kitchen while another questions Lena in the living room. Lena describes how Curtis shoved her into the heater and punched her. The officer then has her write and sign a “battery affidavit.”

Curtis is charged with domestic battery. Lena is subpoenaed but does not appear, and the prosecution cannot locate her. The prosecution calls the officer to recount Lena’s oral statements and offers the affidavit. Curtis objects under the Confrontation Clause.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit both, because Lena’s statements qualify as excited utterances, and a firmly rooted hearsay exception satisfies the Confrontation Clause.
Admit the oral statements but exclude the affidavit, because only formalized, sworn statements are testimonial.
Exclude both, because the primary purpose of the questioning was to establish past events for a possible prosecution, not to meet an ongoing emergency.
Admit both, because Lena is the alleged victim, and the Confrontation Clause is directed at accusatory statements by accomplices and other suspects.
Exclude both unless the prosecution proves Lena is unavailable, in which case both are admissible.
e: Rule: The Confrontation Clause bars testimonial statements of a witness who does not appear at trial unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Crawford v. Washington. Statements to police are testimonial when the circumstances objectively indicate that there is no ongoing emergency and the primary purpose of the interrogation is to establish or prove past events potentially relevant to later prosecution. Davis v. Washington; Hammon v. Indiana.
oe: The “firmly rooted exception” test comes from Ohio v. Roberts, which Crawford overruled for testimonial statements. Qualifying as an excited utterance does not answer the Confrontation question.
Hammon held the oral statements testimonial too. Formality matters, but a structured police interview about past events is formal enough without an oath.
Correct. With the emergency over and the questioning directed at past events, the statements are testimonial under Davis and Hammon.
The Clause protects against all testimonial statements of absent witnesses, whatever the declarant’s role. Victims’ statements to police are the paradigm case.
Unavailability alone is not enough. Crawford requires both unavailability and a prior opportunity for cross-examination.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — Crawford v. Washington · Davis v. Washington

q:
Dalton is charged with sexually abusing his eight-year-old daughter, M., on a military base. M. and her mother lived with Dalton until a bitter custody fight began in January, when Dalton sought sole custody. M. testifies to the abuse. On cross-examination, defense counsel suggests that M.’s mother has coached her since January to fabricate the accusations so that the mother would win custody.

The prosecution then calls M.’s babysitter, who testifies that in March, M. told her the same account M. gave on the stand. The defense objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the babysitter’s testimony as substantive evidence, because the 2014 amendment to Rule 801(d)(1)(B) eliminated the requirement that a consistent statement precede the alleged motive to fabricate.
Exclude the testimony under Rule 801(d)(1)(B), because M.’s statement was made after the alleged motive to fabricate arose.
Admit the testimony only to rehabilitate M.’s credibility, not as substantive evidence of the abuse.
Admit the testimony, because M. testified and is subject to cross-examination about the prior statement, which is all Rule 801(d)(1) requires.
Exclude the testimony, because a prior consistent statement is admissible only if it was given under penalty of perjury.
e: Rule: A testifying declarant’s prior consistent statement is not hearsay if offered (i) to rebut an express or implied charge that the declarant recently fabricated it or acted from a recent improper influence or motive, or (ii) to rehabilitate the declarant’s credibility when attacked on another ground. FRE 801(d)(1)(B). Under Tome v. United States, a statement offered under clause (i) must have been made before the alleged improper motive arose.
oe: The 2014 amendment did not disturb Tome. It extended substantive use to consistent statements that rehabilitate on other grounds, and the note says the premotive rule still governs fabrication charges.
Correct. Under Tome, a consistent statement offered to rebut a charge of improper influence must predate that influence.
Since 2014, a statement that properly rehabilitates under 801(d)(1)(B) comes in substantively. And a post-motive statement does not rehabilitate against a fabrication charge at all.
Being subject to cross is necessary but not sufficient. Clause (B) also requires the statement to be offered for a permitted purpose and, under Tome, to predate the motive.
The oath requirement applies only to prior inconsistent statements under 801(d)(1)(A).
topic: Prior statements & impeachment — FRE 801(d)(1)(B) · Tome v. United States

q:
Fenwick died testate. His executor sues Fenwick’s nephew, Gil, to recover $60,000, alleging that Fenwick lent Gil the money. Gil contends it was a gift. The executor calls Fenwick’s housekeeper, who will testify that she watched Fenwick hand Gil a cashier’s check and say: “This is a loan, not a present. You’ll pay it back when the restaurant turns a profit.” Gil objects on hearsay grounds.

What is the strongest basis for admitting the housekeeper’s testimony?
o: It is an opposing-party statement, because Fenwick’s estate is a party to the action and Fenwick’s statements are attributable to it.
It is a statement against interest, because Fenwick is unavailable and characterizing the transfer as a loan exposed him to tax liability on the interest.
It is admissible under Rule 803(3) as a statement of Fenwick’s memory of the terms on which he had agreed to transfer the money.
It is admissible under the residual exception, because no specific exception applies and the statement was made at the moment of the transfer.
It is not hearsay, because Fenwick’s words accompanying the transfer are legally operative: they help determine whether the transfer was a loan or a gift, regardless of their truth.
e: Rule: Words that have independent legal significance, sometimes called verbal acts or legally operative words, are not hearsay. Examples include the words of an offer or acceptance, a defamatory statement in a defamation case, and words that accompany and characterize a transfer of property. They are offered because they were said, not to prove the truth of anything asserted.
oe: Rule 801(d)(2) admits statements only when offered against the party. Here the executor, standing in Fenwick’s shoes, is offering Fenwick’s statement for itself.
Calling the transfer a loan created a $60,000 asset for Fenwick, which is in his pecuniary favor. Speculative tax consequences do not make it a statement a reasonable person would make only if true.
Rule 803(3) expressly excludes statements of memory or belief offered to prove the fact remembered. Fenwick was also not describing a memory; he was characterizing the transfer as it happened.
Rule 807 is a last resort that requires notice and special findings. There is no need to reach it when the words are not hearsay.
Correct. Words that accompany and characterize a transaction are legally operative and are not offered for their truth.
topic: Definition & non-truth uses — FRE 801(c) · Verbal acts

q:
Nineteen-year-old Lark disappears. At 6:30 p.m. on the night she vanished, she told a friend: “I’m meeting Brody at the Taco Hut lot at nine to pick up some weed. He says he’s got a good deal.” Lark was never seen again.

At Brody’s federal kidnapping trial, the prosecution offers the friend’s testimony to prove (1) that Lark went to the Taco Hut lot and (2) that Brody met her there. Brody objects.

Which statement most accurately describes the admissibility of Lark’s statement?
o: It is inadmissible for any purpose, because Lark’s reference to what Brody “says” is a statement of memory about a past conversation.
It is admissible for both purposes without limitation, because Rule 803(3) admits any statement of a declarant’s then-existing intent.
It is inadmissible, because the statement-of-intent exception applies only when the declarant is unavailable, and the prosecution has not proven that Lark is dead.

It is admissible to prove that Lark went to the lot. Its use to prove Brody’s conduct is contested: the House Judiciary Committee disapproved that use, but many courts permit it, often requiring independent evidence of the other person’s involvement.
It is admissible to prove that Brody met Lark, but not to prove Lark’s own conduct, because a declarant’s stated intentions do not reliably predict her own behavior.
e: Rule: A statement of the declarant’s then-existing state of mind, such as intent or plan, is admissible. FRE 803(3). Under Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Hillmon, a statement of intent is admissible to show that the declarant likely acted on it. Whether it may also prove the conduct of a third person named in the statement is disputed.
oe: The embedded statement is Brody’s own, admissible against him under 801(d)(2)(A). Lark’s main assertion looks forward, not backward.
This overstates the rule. Using one person’s stated intent to prove another person’s conduct is the contested part, and the legislative history cuts against it.
Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of the declarant’s availability.
Correct. This states the Hillmon rule and the current split over the Pheaster use.
This reverses the doctrine. The declarant’s own future conduct is the uncontroversial use; the third party’s conduct is the contested one.
topic: 803: spontaneity, state of mind, medical — FRE 803(3) · Mutual Life Ins. Co. v. Hillmon

q:
DEA Agent Pratt, posing as a buyer, records a meeting at which Quill sells her half a kilogram of cocaine. During the deal, Quill says: “You want more, I can get it. My guy is Ferris. He drives it up from Miami every other Thursday. Buy two keys and he’ll knock off ten percent.” Two weeks later, agents watch Ferris’s car arrive at Quill’s house on a Thursday night. Ferris carries a gym bag inside and leaves without it.

Quill is never charged. At Ferris’s trial for conspiracy to distribute cocaine, the prosecution offers Quill’s recorded statement. Ferris objects.

How should the court proceed?
o: Admit the statement if the judge finds by a preponderance of the evidence, considering the statement itself together with the surveillance evidence, that Quill and Ferris were members of a conspiracy and that Quill made the statement during and in furtherance of it.
Exclude the statement, because Agent Pratt, as a government agent, was not a member of the conspiracy, so a statement to her could not further it.
Admit the statement only if evidence other than the statement itself establishes the conspiracy and Ferris’s membership in it by a preponderance of the evidence.
Submit the preliminary question to the jury, instructing it to disregard the statement unless it finds beyond a reasonable doubt that Ferris and Quill were co-conspirators.
Exclude the statement, because Quill was never charged, and a co-conspirator’s statement is admissible only against a co-defendant charged in the same conspiracy.
e: Rule: A statement by a party’s co-conspirator made during and in furtherance of the conspiracy is not hearsay when offered against that party. FRE 801(d)(2)(E). The court decides the preliminary facts under Rule 104(a) by a preponderance of the evidence and may consider the statement itself. Bourjaily v. United States. But the statement alone does not establish the existence of the conspiracy or the party’s participation in it. FRE 801(d)(2) (final sentence).
oe: Correct. This is the Bourjaily standard as codified: the judge decides by a preponderance, may consider the statement, and needs some corroborating evidence.
The listener need not be a conspirator. Statements made to recruit, reassure, or induce a buyer, even one who turns out to be an agent, can further the conspiracy.
This is the pre-Bourjaily independent-evidence rule. The court may consider the statement itself, though it cannot rely on it alone.
Preliminary questions of admissibility under 801(d)(2)(E) are for the judge under Rule 104(a), decided by a preponderance, not for the jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
The co-conspirator need not be charged, tried, or even identified, as long as the court finds the conspiracy and both memberships.
topic: Opposing-party statements — FRE 801(d)(2)(E) · FRE 104(a)

q:
Dock supervisor Weller saw a box truck pull away from a loading bay moments after a pallet of laptops was stolen. While the truck was still in view, she wrote its license plate number on the back of a shipping invoice.

At the thief’s trial eleven months later, Weller testifies that she wrote the number down accurately while looking at the truck, but that she cannot remember the number now, even after looking at the invoice. The prosecution moves to admit the invoice and hand it to the jury.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the invoice as an exhibit, because it satisfies the recorded-recollection exception.
Permit the notation to be read into evidence, but do not receive the invoice itself as an exhibit unless the defense offers it.
Exclude the invoice, because a writing that fails to refresh a witness’s memory cannot be used for any purpose.
Exclude the invoice, because Weller remembers the theft, and the recorded-recollection exception applies only when the witness has no memory of the events.
Admit the invoice as a business record, because it was written on a company form during the workday.
e: Rule: A recorded recollection is admissible if it is a record that (A) is on a matter the witness once knew about but now cannot recall well enough to testify fully and accurately; (B) was made or adopted by the witness when the matter was fresh in the witness’s memory; and (C) accurately reflects the witness’s knowledge. If admitted, the record may be read into evidence but may be received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party. FRE 803(5).
oe: The rule permits the record to be read into evidence, but only the adverse party may introduce it as an exhibit.
Correct. This is the final sentence of Rule 803(5).
Failure to refresh is exactly what triggers Rule 803(5). Refreshing under Rule 612 and recorded recollection are separate tools.
The standard is insufficient memory to testify fully and accurately about the matter recorded, here the plate number. Total amnesia about the events is not required.
One supervisor’s ad hoc notation of a plate is not a record of a regularly conducted activity made as a regular practice. Rule 803(6) does not fit.
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 803(5) · FRE 612

q:
Ames sues a property owner for the drowning death of her son, Jace, at an unfenced retention pond. Three hours after the drowning, after Teo, Jace’s nine-year-old playmate, had stopped crying and was sitting calmly with a neighbor, Teo told the neighbor: “Jace slipped on the broken boards by the pond. The fence part was missing.” Teo’s family has since moved abroad and cannot be reached. Photographs taken that evening show missing fence panels and broken boards exactly where Teo said.

Two weeks before trial, Ames served written notice identifying Teo, the neighbor, and the substance of the statement, and stating that she would offer it under the residual exception. The court finds that the statement is not an excited utterance. The owner objects.

Which is the most accurate statement of the court’s authority?
o: The court must exclude the statement, because the residual exception may not be used to admit a statement that nearly misses a specific exception such as Rule 803(2).

The court must exclude the statement, because Rule 807 requires circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness equivalent to those of the enumerated exceptions, and a child’s statement made after reflection cannot meet that standard.
The court may admit the statement only if Ames also shows that Teo is unavailable, because Rule 807 is limited to unavailable declarants.

The court may admit the statement if it finds sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness, considering the totality of the circumstances and the corroborating photographs, and that the statement is more probative on the point than any other evidence Ames can obtain through reasonable efforts.
The court may not admit the statement, because notice under Rule 807 must be served at least 30 days before trial.
e: Rule: A hearsay statement not admissible under Rule 803 or 804 may be admitted if (1) it is supported by sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness, after considering the totality of circumstances under which it was made and any evidence corroborating it; and (2) it is more probative on the point for which it is offered than any other evidence the proponent can obtain through reasonable efforts. The proponent must give reasonable notice in writing before trial, including the substance of the statement and the declarant’s name. FRE 807 (as amended 2019).
oe: The 2019 committee note rejects the near-miss theory. A statement may come in under Rule 807 even if it narrowly fails a specific exception.
The “equivalent guarantees” language was deleted in 2019, and no category of declarant is categorically excluded.
Rule 807 has no unavailability requirement. Availability can matter only to whether the statement is more probative than other obtainable evidence.
Correct. This tracks the current text of Rule 807.
Rule 807 requires reasonable notice in writing before trial, or during trial if the court excuses the lack of earlier notice for good cause. There is no fixed 30-day period.
topic: Residual, multiple hearsay, completeness — FRE 807 · 2019 Advisory Committee Note

q:
Dwayne is charged with murdering his former girlfriend, Brenda, by shooting her during an argument in her driveway. Three weeks earlier, Brenda gave a recorded interview to a detective at the police station in which she said that Dwayne had choked her and threatened to kill her if she “ever went to the cops again.”

The prosecution offers the recorded interview, arguing that Dwayne forfeited his confrontation right by killing Brenda. Apart from the earlier threat, there is no evidence of why Dwayne shot her other than the argument itself.

What must the court find before admitting the interview over a Confrontation Clause objection?
o: Only that Dwayne killed Brenda, by a preponderance of the evidence, because a defendant whose wrongdoing makes a witness unavailable forfeits the right to confront her.
That Dwayne killed Brenda, beyond a reasonable doubt, because the forfeiture finding overlaps with the ultimate issue the jury must decide.
Nothing further, because statements describing threats of violence are not testimonial.
That Brenda’s statement bears adequate indicia of reliability, because forfeiture is an equitable doctrine concerned with the trustworthiness of the evidence.
That Dwayne engaged in wrongdoing designed, at least in part, to prevent Brenda from testifying, a finding that evidence of his threat to harm her if she went to the police may help support.
e: Rule: Forfeiture by wrongdoing applies only when the defendant engaged in conduct designed to prevent the witness from testifying. Giles v. California. Rule 804(b)(6) likewise requires that the party wrongfully caused or acquiesced in causing the declarant’s unavailability “and did so intending that result.” Federal courts apply a preponderance standard.
oe: Giles rejected forfeiture based on the killing alone. The defendant must have intended to prevent testimony.
Federal courts use a preponderance standard for the forfeiture finding, as under Rule 104(a). The Supreme Court in Davis noted that practice.
A recorded station-house interview narrating past abuse is testimonial. Its subject matter does not change that.
Reliability-based confrontation analysis is the Ohio v. Roberts approach that Crawford rejected. Forfeiture turns on the defendant’s wrongdoing and intent, not on the statement’s reliability.
Correct. Giles requires intent to prevent testimony, and the threat about going to the police is strong evidence of it.
topic: 804: declarant unavailable — Giles v. California · FRE 804(b)(6)

q:
Dorsey is charged with murdering Vic and claims self-defense. Two days after the shooting, eyewitness Wren gave police an unsworn, signed written statement: “Vic’s hands were empty and raised when Dorsey shot him.” A month later, Wren gave the same account under oath before a grand jury.

At trial, Wren testifies that Vic lunged at Dorsey with a knife before Dorsey fired. The prosecution offers both prior statements.

For what purposes may the jury consider them?
o: Both may be considered as substantive evidence, because Wren is testifying and is subject to cross-examination about them.
Neither may be considered as substantive evidence, because the grand jury proceeding lacked cross-examination and the police statement lacked an oath.
The grand jury testimony may be considered both to impeach Wren and as substantive evidence; the police statement may be considered only to impeach Wren.
Both may be considered only to impeach Wren, because a prior inconsistent statement is substantive evidence only if the declarant was cross-examined when it was made.
The police statement may be considered as substantive evidence, because Wren’s signature is the functional equivalent of an oath; the grand jury testimony may be considered only to impeach.
e: Rule: A testifying declarant’s prior inconsistent statement is not hearsay if it was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding, or in a deposition. FRE 801(d)(1)(A). Other inconsistent statements may be used only to impeach, with a limiting instruction on request. FRE 613; FRE 105.
oe: Being subject to cross at trial is necessary but not sufficient. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) also requires that the prior statement have been made under penalty of perjury in a proceeding.
Cross-examination when the statement was made is not required. The rule’s text requires only an oath in a proceeding, and grand jury testimony satisfies it.
Correct. The sworn grand jury testimony is substantive evidence; the unsworn police statement only impeaches.
This states the rule Congress rejected. The final rule requires an oath and a proceeding, not contemporaneous cross-examination.
A signature does not substitute for “penalty of perjury” in a proceeding. It is the grand jury testimony, not the police statement, that qualifies.
topic: Prior statements & impeachment — FRE 801(d)(1)(A) · FRE 613

q:
Dunn is prosecuted for aggravated driving while intoxicated. Analyst Dorrance ran Dunn’s blood sample through a gas chromatograph and signed a “Certificate of Analyst” reporting a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.21 and affirming that the sample’s seal was intact, that he followed the lab’s protocol, and that no circumstance affected the sample’s integrity. Before trial, Dorrance is placed on unpaid leave for undisclosed reasons.

The prosecution calls analyst Petrakis, who works in the same lab and knows its procedures but did not observe or review Dorrance’s test, to introduce the certificate. Dunn objects.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude the certificate, because it is testimonial and Dunn has the right to confront the analyst who made the certification, not a surrogate.
Admit the certificate, because Petrakis is subject to full cross-examination about the lab’s procedures and the reliability of gas chromatography.
Admit the certificate, because Dorrance merely transcribed a machine’s output, and machine output is not a statement by a person.
Admit the certificate as a business record, because the lab regularly prepares such certificates and business records are nontestimonial.
Admit the certificate, because Dunn could have subpoenaed Dorrance himself if he wanted to cross-examine him.
e: Rule: Forensic reports created to serve as evidence in a criminal prosecution are testimonial. Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts. The Confrontation Clause is not satisfied by surrogate testimony from an analyst who did not perform or observe the test reported in the certification. Bullcoming v. New Mexico.
oe: Correct. This is Bullcoming: the certifying analyst must be made available, absent unavailability and a prior opportunity for cross.
Bullcoming rejected surrogate testimony. Cross about general procedures does not test what the certifying analyst did and saw.
The certificate conveyed the analyst’s own representations about chain of custody and protocol, not raw machine output.
Records made for the purpose of proving a fact at trial are testimonial even if routinely made. Melendez-Diaz rejected the business-record argument for exactly this kind of document.
Melendez-Diaz held that the prosecution bears the burden of presenting its witnesses. The defendant’s subpoena power does not substitute for confrontation.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — Bullcoming v. New Mexico · Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts

q:
In a prosecution for armed robbery of a convenience store, the clerk who was robbed has died of unrelated causes before trial. The prosecution offers each of the following items of evidence.

Which item is hearsay?
o: A printout from the store’s cash register showing a “No Sale” drawer opening at 11:42 p.m.
An officer’s testimony that when she knocked at the defendant’s apartment door and announced “Police!”, the defendant jumped out of a rear window.
Testimony that during the citywide search for the robber, the defendant’s sister bought him a one-way bus ticket to Mexico.
A detective’s testimony that, at a lineup the day after the robbery, the clerk pointed to the defendant when asked to identify the robber.
Testimony that, the morning after the robbery, the defendant told a friend, “I’m the guy who hit the QuickMart.”
e: Rule: A statement includes nonverbal conduct if the person intended it as an assertion. FRE 801(a). Only a “person” makes a statement. Statements by an opposing party are excluded from the hearsay definition. FRE 801(d)(2). A prior identification is excluded only if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination. FRE 801(d)(1)(C).
oe: Machine-generated data is not a statement by a person. The register printout raises authentication issues under Rule 901(b)(9), not hearsay.
Flight is offered as circumstantial evidence of consciousness of guilt. The defendant did not intend to assert anything by jumping out the window.
The sister’s purchase may imply a belief that her brother needed to flee, but she did not intend it as an assertion. Under the Federal Rules, nonassertive conduct is not hearsay.
Correct. The pointing is intended as an assertion, and the 801(d)(1)(C) exclusion is unavailable because the declarant does not testify.
This is the defendant’s own statement offered against him, so it is not hearsay under 801(d)(2)(A).
topic: Definition & non-truth uses — FRE 801(a) · FRE 801(d)(1)(C)

q:
At 3:25 a.m., officers responding to a “man down” call find Rico lying in a gas station parking lot with a gunshot wound to the abdomen, in obvious pain and having difficulty breathing. The shooting happened about 25 minutes earlier, six blocks away; Rico drove himself to the station. Before the paramedics arrive, officers ask, “What happened? Who shot you? Where did it happen?” Rico answers: “Bricks shot me, through the back door of his house on Seventh. I was talking to him through the door and he shot.”

Rico survives, but at Bramlett’s (“Bricks”) trial for attempted murder, Rico refuses to testify despite a court order and a contempt citation. The prosecution offers the officers’ testimony repeating Rico’s answers. Bramlett objects on hearsay and Confrontation Clause grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude the statements, because statements made in response to police questioning cannot be excited utterances.
Admit the statements, because they are excited utterances and, with an armed shooter whose location and motive were unknown, the primary purpose of the exchange was to meet an ongoing emergency.
Admit the statements as dying declarations, because Rico’s grave wound shows that he believed he was dying.
Exclude the statements, because 25 minutes had passed and Rico had driven six blocks, so the statements were the product of reflection.
Exclude the statements, because statements identifying a perpetrator to police are testimonial per se.
e: Rule: An excited utterance is a statement relating to a startling event made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement it caused. FRE 803(2). Statements to police are nontestimonial when, viewed objectively from the perspectives of both the declarant and the questioners, their primary purpose is to enable police to meet an ongoing emergency. Michigan v. Bryant. A dying declaration is admissible only in a homicide prosecution or a civil case. FRE 804(b)(2).
oe: Responding to a question does not destroy spontaneity. Courts routinely admit excited answers to questions like “What happened?”
Correct. This is the Bryant analysis paired with a straightforward Rule 803(2) foundation.
Rule 804(b)(2) applies only in homicide prosecutions and civil cases. This is a prosecution for attempted murder. The record also does not show that Rico believed death was imminent.
There is no fixed time limit for excited utterances. The question is whether the declarant was still under the stress of the event, and Rico plainly was.
Bryant rejected any per se rule. Identification of an armed assailant at large can serve the emergency purpose.
topic: 803: spontaneity, state of mind, medical — FRE 803(2) · Michigan v. Bryant

q:
Six days before a fatal collision, Ostrander told his mechanic: “The brakes have been grabbing and fading for a month, but I’m not paying for new rotors until after the holidays.” Ostrander was killed in the collision, which also injured Pell.

Pell sues Ostrander’s estate for negligence and calls the mechanic to repeat Ostrander’s statement. The estate objects. The trial takes place in 2026.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because a decedent’s statements are not attributable to the decedent’s estate.
Admit it as a statement against interest, because Ostrander is unavailable and the statement exposed him to civil liability.
Admit it under Rule 803(3), because it reflects Ostrander’s then-existing intent to postpone the repair.
Exclude it, because the only potentially applicable exception is the statement-against-interest exception, and the statement was not against Ostrander’s interest when he made it.
Admit it as an opposing-party statement, because the estate’s potential liability is directly derived from Ostrander, and the statement would have been admissible against Ostrander himself.
e: Rule: As amended effective December 1, 2024, Rule 801(d)(2) provides: “If a party’s claim, defense, or potential liability is directly derived from a declarant or the declarant’s principal, a statement that would be admissible against the declarant or the principal under this rule is also admissible against the party.”
oe: This was the minority view before 2024. The amended rule now attributes the statement to a party whose liability derives from the declarant.
Against-interest status is measured when the statement is made. Before any accident, describing worn brakes did not expose Ostrander to any realistic liability.
Rule 803(3) reaches the forward-looking intent to delay repairs, but not the backward-looking assertion that the brakes had been failing for a month, which is the important part.
This ignores the 2024 amendment to Rule 801(d)(2), which supplies a route that does not depend on the statement being against interest.
Correct. The 2024 amendment makes the decedent’s statement admissible against the estate whose liability derives from him.
topic: Opposing-party statements — FRE 801(d)(2) (2024 amendment) · FRE 804(b)(3)

q:
Ibarra is charged with illegal reentry after removal, which requires proof that he did not obtain the government’s consent to reapply for admission. Three weeks before trial, the prosecutor serves written notice that it intends to offer a “Certificate of Nonexistence of Record,” signed by a Department of Homeland Security records custodian, attesting that a diligent search of the agency’s databases found no record that Ibarra applied for or received consent to reenter. Ibarra’s lawyer files nothing in response.

At trial, the custodian is not present, and Ibarra objects to the certificate under the Confrontation Clause.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the certificate, because Ibarra did not object in writing within 7 days after receiving the notice.
Admit the certificate, because a certificate attesting to the absence of a record is not testimonial; it merely reflects the contents of public records.
Exclude the certificate, because the Confrontation Clause requires the custodian’s live testimony whenever such a certificate is offered against the accused, regardless of notice.
Exclude the certificate, because evidence of the absence of a public record is admissible only in civil cases.
Admit the certificate, because Ibarra’s lawyer could have subpoenaed the custodian.
e: Rule: Testimony or a certification that a diligent search failed to disclose a public record is admissible to prove that the record does not exist. In a criminal case, a prosecutor who intends to offer a certification must give written notice at least 14 days before trial, and the certification is admissible if the defendant does not object in writing within 7 days of receiving the notice, unless the court sets a different time. FRE 803(10).
oe: Correct. Rule 803(10)(B)’s notice-and-demand procedure was satisfied, and Ibarra waived his objection by not demanding the custodian.
Certificates of nonexistence of record are treated as testimonial after Melendez-Diaz. That is why the 2013 notice-and-demand amendment was needed.
Melendez-Diaz approved notice-and-demand statutes. A defendant can forfeit the right to live testimony by failing to make a timely demand.
Rule 803(10) applies in criminal cases, with the added notice procedure.
Melendez-Diaz rejected the idea that the defendant’s subpoena power satisfies the Confrontation Clause. The waiver here comes from the notice-and-demand procedure, not from subpoena power.
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 803(10) · Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts

q:
In each scenario below, a party offers a hearsay statement under a Rule 804(b) exception.

In which scenario does the declarant fail to qualify as “unavailable”?
o: The declarant appears at trial, invokes her Fifth Amendment privilege, and the court sustains the claim. Her statement is offered under Rule 804(b)(3).
The declarant takes the stand but refuses to answer questions about the subject matter, despite a court order and a contempt citation. His statement is offered under Rule 804(b)(1).

The declarant, a Portuguese citizen living in Lisbon, refuses the proponent’s requests to come to trial. The proponent never tried to take her deposition. Her statement is offered under Rule 804(b)(3).
The declarant, a Portuguese citizen living in Lisbon, refuses the proponent’s repeated requests to come to trial. Her former testimony is offered under Rule 804(b)(1).
The declarant testifies credibly that he has no memory of the subject matter of his statement. His statement is offered under Rule 804(b)(2).
e: Rule: A declarant is unavailable if exempted by privilege, refuses to testify despite a court order, testifies to not remembering the subject matter, cannot be present because of death or illness, or is absent and the proponent has been unable, by process or other reasonable means, to procure (A) the declarant’s attendance, for Rule 804(b)(1) or (6); or (B) the declarant’s attendance or testimony, for Rule 804(b)(2), (3), or (4). FRE 804(a).
oe: A sustained privilege claim makes the declarant unavailable under 804(a)(1).
Persistent refusal despite a court order makes the declarant unavailable under 804(a)(2).
Correct. For 804(b)(3), Rule 804(a)(5)(B) requires reasonable efforts to procure the declarant’s testimony, such as a deposition, as well as attendance.
For 804(b)(1), Rule 804(a)(5)(A) requires only reasonable efforts to procure attendance, and a foreign national abroad is beyond the court’s subpoena power.
Lack of memory of the subject matter makes the declarant unavailable under 804(a)(3).
topic: 804: declarant unavailable — FRE 804(a)(1)–(5) · FRE 804(b)

q:
In Jason’s drug-possession trial, the state crime-lab analyst who tested the seized substance, Rast, no longer works at the lab. Rast’s notes and report, prepared after police requested testing for Jason’s case, record the tests she ran and that the results indicated methamphetamine.

The prosecution calls a substitute expert, Longoni, who never saw the substance. Longoni tells the jury what Rast’s notes say about the tests performed and their results, then gives her “independent opinion” that the substance was methamphetamine. The prosecution argues that Rast’s notes were offered not for their truth but only to show the basis of Longoni’s opinion under Rule 703. Jason objects under the Confrontation Clause.

Under current Supreme Court precedent, which statement is most accurate?
o: There is no Confrontation problem, because basis evidence disclosed under Rule 703 is not offered for its truth.
There is no Confrontation problem, because Longoni offered her own independent opinion and was available for cross-examination.
There is a Confrontation violation whether or not Rast’s notes are testimonial, because any out-of-court statement an expert relays to the jury is subject to the Clause.
Rast’s statements were offered for their truth, because they supported Longoni’s opinion only if true; whether admitting them violated the Clause depends on whether they were testimonial.
There is a Confrontation violation only if Longoni failed to review Rast’s raw data independently before testifying.
e: Rule: When an expert conveys an absent analyst’s statements in support of the expert’s opinion, and the statements provide that support only if they are true, the statements come into evidence for their truth. Smith v. Arizona (2024). The Confrontation Clause then bars them if they are testimonial.
oe: Smith rejected this theory. Basis testimony that supports the opinion only if true is offered for its truth.
An expert’s independent opinion does not launder the absent analyst’s statements she relays to the jury. Cross-examining Longoni cannot test what Rast did.
The Clause applies only to testimonial statements. Smith left the testimonial question open on remand.
Correct. This is the holding of Smith v. Arizona and the question it left for remand.
The problem is what Longoni told the jury Rast said, not how carefully Longoni prepared.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — Smith v. Arizona (2024) · FRE 703

q:
Dove sues Kessler for injuries from an intersection collision. Kessler testifies on direct examination that his light was green. Dove’s counsel does not cross-examine Kessler about anything he said before trial.

After Kessler leaves the stand and the defense rests, Dove offers in rebuttal an email that Kessler sent his insurer the day after the crash: “Honestly I think I might have run the red. I was looking at my GPS.” Kessler objects, citing Rule 613(b) as amended in 2024.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude the email, because extrinsic evidence of a witness’s prior inconsistent statement may not be admitted until the witness has been given an opportunity to explain or deny it.
Admit the email as substantive evidence, because Rule 613(b)’s foundation requirement does not apply to an opposing party’s statement under Rule 801(d)(2).
Admit the email, but only to impeach Kessler’s credibility, with a limiting instruction.
Exclude the email, because it was sent to Kessler’s liability insurer, and Rule 411 bars evidence of insurance.
Admit the email only if Dove recalls Kessler to the stand so he can explain or deny it.
e: Rule: Unless the court orders otherwise, extrinsic evidence of a witness’s prior inconsistent statement may not be admitted until after the witness is given an opportunity to explain or deny it and an adverse party is given an opportunity to examine the witness about it. This subdivision does not apply to an opposing party’s statement under Rule 801(d)(2). FRE 613(b) (as amended 2024).
oe: This is the 2024 rule for ordinary witnesses, but the rule’s last sentence exempts opposing-party statements.
Correct. A party’s own statement is substantive evidence, and Rule 613(b)’s foundation requirement does not apply to it.
Kessler’s email is admissible for its truth under 801(d)(2)(A), not just to impeach.
Rule 411 bars insurance evidence only when offered to prove negligence or wrongful conduct. The email is offered for what Kessler admitted, and any reference to insurance can be redacted.
No foundation is required for an opposing party’s statement, so Dove need not recall Kessler.
topic: Prior statements & impeachment — FRE 613(b) (2024 amendment) · FRE 801(d)(2)(A)

q:
Dr. Halloway is charged with murdering his wife, Corinne, by poisoning her with a compound found in his laboratory. The defense contends that Corinne committed suicide. Two weeks before her death, while bedridden but improving, Corinne asked her nurse to bring a bottle of whiskey from Dr. Halloway’s closet. After sipping it, she said it tasted strange, then said: “Dr. Halloway has poisoned me.”

The prosecution concedes that Corinne did not believe she was about to die. It offers the statement only to show her state of mind: that she had the will to live and was not suicidal.

What is the best ruling?
o: Admit the statement under Rule 803(3) with a limiting instruction, because it is offered only to show Corinne’s then-existing state of mind.
Admit the statement as a dying declaration, because Corinne died within two weeks of making it.

Exclude the statement, because its real force is as an accusation of a past act; the state-of-mind exception does not admit statements of memory or belief to prove the fact believed, and a limiting instruction cannot realistically confine the jury.
Admit the statement under Rule 803(4), because it was made to a nurse and identified the cause of Corinne’s symptoms.
Exclude the statement, because a homicide victim’s statements are admissible only under the dying-declaration exception.
e: Rule: Rule 803(3) admits a statement of the declarant’s then-existing state of mind but not “a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed.” When the legitimate state-of-mind use is slight and the forbidden use is overwhelming, the court should exclude under Rule 403. Shepard v. United States.
oe: This is the argument Shepard rejected. The forbidden inference from a backward-looking accusation overwhelms the permitted state-of-mind use.
A dying declaration requires that the declarant believe death is imminent, and the prosecution concedes she did not.
Correct. This is the Shepard reasoning, reflected in Rule 803(3)’s exclusion and Rule 403.
The statement was not made for diagnosis or treatment, and who caused the poisoning is not reasonably pertinent to treating it.
Overbroad. A homicide victim’s statements can come in under many exceptions, such as 803(1), 803(2), and 803(3) for forward-looking intent.
topic: 803: spontaneity, state of mind, medical — FRE 803(3) · Shepard v. United States

q:
In a wrongful-death suit against Calder Chemical after a plant explosion, the plaintiff offers an internal email that Calder plant engineer Yost sent a coworker a week before the explosion: “My supervisor Mona told me this morning that the CEO said, quote, ‘Pull the pressure-valve inspection reports from the file before the state auditors get here.’”

Yost, Mona, and the CEO were all Calder employees at the time. Yost knows what the CEO said only through Mona. Calder objects on hearsay grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude the email, because a statement within a statement is admissible only if every declarant is unavailable.
Exclude the email, because Rule 801(d)(2)(D) requires that the employee have personal knowledge of the matter, and Yost had none.
Admit Yost’s own words, but redact the quotation attributed to the CEO.
Exclude the email, because Mona’s statement is double hearsay, and double hearsay is inadmissible unless a single exception covers both layers.

Admit the email, because each layer is excluded from the hearsay rule: the CEO’s instruction is an opposing-party statement and, as a directive, not an assertion at all; Yost’s and Mona’s statements are by Calder employees on matters within the scope of their employment, made while employed.
e: Rule: Hearsay within hearsay is not excluded if each part of the combined statements conforms with an exception. FRE 805. Courts apply the same principle to the 801(d)(2) exclusions. Statements by a party’s employees on matters within the scope of their employment, made during the relationship, are not hearsay against the party, and the declarant need not have personal knowledge. FRE 801(d)(2)(D).
oe: Rule 805 requires only that each layer satisfy an exception or exclusion. It has no unavailability requirement.
The advisory committee note frees party admissions, including employee statements under 801(d)(2)(D), from the personal-knowledge requirement.
The CEO’s words need no redaction: they are both a nonassertive directive and a party statement.
Each layer needs its own basis; one exception need not cover both. Here, each layer has one.
Correct. Every layer is excluded from the hearsay rule, so Rule 805 is satisfied.
topic: Residual, multiple hearsay, completeness — FRE 805 · FRE 801(d)(2)(D)

q:
Seven-year-old Nora was lured from a playground into a stranger’s house and assaulted. When she got home an hour later, she described the place to her mother: a front room with a green couch, a fish tank with one large orange fish, a staircase with a broken bottom step, and a picture of a white horse over the fireplace.

Nora does not testify at the defendant’s trial. The prosecution calls the mother to repeat the description, and a detective then testifies that the defendant’s house, where Nora had never been before that day, contains each of those features. The defendant objects to the mother’s testimony as hearsay.

What is the best argument for admitting the mother’s testimony?
o: The description is not offered to prove that the house had those features, which the detective proves independently, but to show that Nora had knowledge she could have acquired only by being inside the defendant’s house.
The description is an excited utterance, because Nora had just been assaulted.
The description is admissible under Rule 803(3) as a statement of Nora’s then-existing state of mind.
The description is a statement of identification, because it identifies the defendant’s house as the place Nora perceived earlier.
The description is a present sense impression, because Nora described the room as she remembered seeing it.
e: Rule: A statement offered as circumstantial evidence of the declarant’s knowledge, rather than to prove the facts it describes, is not offered for the truth of the matter asserted. Bridges v. State.
oe: Correct. The statement is circumstantial evidence of Nora’s knowledge, which is the Bridges theory.
An hour later, at home, giving a detailed description, Nora was not clearly under the stress of the event. This is weaker than the non-hearsay argument.
Rule 803(3) excludes statements of memory offered to prove the fact remembered. A description of a room is memory.
Rule 801(d)(1)(C) applies only if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination. Nora does not testify.
A present sense impression must be made while or immediately after perceiving the event. Nora spoke an hour later, from memory.
topic: Definition & non-truth uses — Bridges v. State · FRE 801(c)

q:
After his arrest, Harlan waived his Miranda rights and told FBI agents in a recorded interview: “Yeah, I moved the kilos through my body shop. But Delacroix was the boss. It was his money, his connect, and he told me who to deliver to.”

At Delacroix’s separate trial for drug conspiracy, Harlan invokes the Fifth Amendment, and the court sustains the claim. The prosecution offers the entire recorded interview against Delacroix.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the entire statement as a co-conspirator statement, because Harlan was describing the structure of the conspiracy.
Admit the entire statement as a statement against Harlan’s penal interest, because the narrative as a whole was self-inculpatory.
Admit only “I moved the kilos through my body shop,” because that portion alone is self-inculpatory.
Admit the statement with a limiting instruction that the jury may consider it only against Harlan.
Exclude the entire statement, because it is testimonial and Delacroix has had no opportunity to cross-examine Harlan.
e: Rule: Rule 804(b)(3) is applied statement by statement; it does not admit non-self-inculpatory statements even if they are made within a broader narrative that is generally self-inculpatory. Williamson v. United States. Independently, the Confrontation Clause bars testimonial statements of an absent declarant whom the defendant has had no opportunity to cross-examine. Crawford v. Washington.
oe: Statements to police after arrest are not made in furtherance of the conspiracy. By then the declarant is cooperating against it, not advancing it.
Williamson rejects treating a whole narrative as against interest. The blame-shifting portions are not self-inculpatory.
This is the right hearsay analysis under Williamson, but the testimonial statement still violates the Confrontation Clause when offered against Delacroix.
Harlan is not a party to this trial. A limiting instruction to use the statement only against him is meaningless here.
Correct. Whatever the hearsay analysis, a testimonial custodial statement by an absent declarant cannot be used against the accused without prior cross-examination.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — FRE 804(b)(3) · Williamson v. United States

q:
Two days after a grade-crossing collision, the locomotive engineer, at his railroad employer’s direction, gave a statement describing the crash to the railroad’s claims agent. The railroad takes such statements after every accident, files them in its claims department, and uses them in settlement negotiations and litigation. The engineer has since died.

In the injured motorist’s suit, the railroad offers the statement as a business record, supported by a qualified custodian’s testimony satisfying Rule 803(6)(A) through (C). The motorist objects.

Which statement best describes how the court should proceed?
o: The court must admit the statement, because the railroad established every foundational element of Rule 803(6), and trustworthiness is not part of the rule.
The court should admit the statement only if the railroad proves affirmatively that it is trustworthy.

The court may exclude the statement if the motorist shows that the source of information or the method or circumstances of preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness, as a statement prepared by an interested party in anticipation of litigation likely does.
The court must exclude the statement, because an employee’s statement about an accident can never be a business record.
The court should admit the statement, but only against the railroad, because it is the railroad’s own employee’s statement.
e: Rule: A record of a regularly conducted activity is admissible if the foundational requirements are met and “the opponent does not show that the source of information or the method or circumstances of preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness.” FRE 803(6)(E). The 2014 amendment placed this burden on the opponent.
oe: Trustworthiness is expressly part of the rule in subsection (E).
Since 2014, the burden is on the opponent to show untrustworthiness, not on the proponent to prove trustworthiness.
Correct. This states the 2014 allocation of the burden and the concern from Palmer v. Hoffman.
There is no categorical bar. Many accident reports qualify. The problem is records prepared in anticipation of litigation, which the court evaluates case by case.

The railroad is offering its own employee’s statement. Rule 801(d)(2) applies only to statements offered against a party, and “only against the railroad” makes no sense when the railroad is the proponent.
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 803(6)(E) · Palmer v. Hoffman

q:
Teddy is on trial for the murder of Vance, who was stabbed in an alley. Paramedics found Vance bleeding heavily. As they worked on him, Vance said: “I’m done for. Tell my mom I love her. Teddy stabbed me over the eight hundred he owes me. And tell the cops Teddy’s the one who killed Ray Moss last summer, too.” Vance died in the ambulance.

The prosecution offers all of Vance’s statement.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit the entire statement as a dying declaration, because Vance believed his death was imminent.
Admit the statements that Teddy stabbed Vance over the money he owed, but exclude the statement about Ray Moss.
Exclude the entire statement, because Vance’s belief that death was imminent must be shown by evidence other than his own words.
Admit only “Teddy stabbed me.” The reference to the debt must be excluded as a statement of motive, which falls outside the exception.
Exclude the entire statement, because statements to paramedics are testimonial and Vance cannot be cross-examined.
e: Rule: In a homicide prosecution or civil case, a statement that the declarant, while believing death to be imminent, made about its cause or circumstances is admissible if the declarant is unavailable. FRE 804(b)(2).
oe: The exception is limited to the cause or circumstances of the declarant’s own death. The Ray Moss accusation is outside it.
Correct. Identity and motive are part of the cause and circumstances; another killing is not.
The declarant’s belief can be proven by his own words together with the nature of his injuries.
“Circumstances” of the death include why the declarant was attacked. Motive is within the exception.
Statements to paramedics during emergency treatment are nontestimonial in purpose, and dying declarations may be a recognized historical exception to the Clause anyway.
topic: 804: declarant unavailable — FRE 804(b)(2) · Giles v. California

q:
At a crowded bar the night after a jewelry-store robbery, Pruitt’s longtime friend Gage said to Pruitt, loudly enough for three others at the table to hear: “You need to lie low, man. The cops are all over town looking for whoever hit Kessel’s Jewelers, and that was some sloppy work you did.” Pruitt shrugged, laughed, and ordered another round. No police were present, and Pruitt had not been arrested or questioned.

At Pruitt’s robbery trial, the prosecution calls one of the others at the table to recount the exchange.

Which statement is most accurate?
o: The testimony is inadmissible, because using a defendant’s silence as evidence of guilt violates the Fifth Amendment and due process.
The testimony is inadmissible, because silence can amount to adoption only when the accusation is made by a police officer.
Gage’s statement is admissible as a co-conspirator statement, because Gage was helping Pruitt avoid detection.

The testimony is admissible as an adoptive admission if the evidence supports findings that Pruitt heard and understood Gage’s statement and that, under the circumstances, a person in Pruitt’s position would have denied it if untrue.
The testimony is admissible only to show Pruitt’s state of mind, and the jury must be instructed not to consider it as evidence that he committed the robbery.
e: Rule: A statement is not hearsay if offered against a party who manifested that it adopted or believed it to be true. FRE 801(d)(2)(B). Silence can be an adoption when the party heard and understood the statement, was able to respond, and, under the circumstances, would naturally have denied it if it were untrue.
oe: Doyle bars the use of post-Miranda silence. Pre-arrest silence in response to a private person’s accusation raises no Fifth Amendment or due process problem.
Adoption by silence most often arises with private accusers. Police accusations, especially after arrest, are actually more problematic.
There is no evidence that Gage was a co-conspirator in the robbery, and after-the-fact advice to lie low is not in furtherance of a conspiracy shown here.
Correct. This states the adoptive-admission test for silence.
An adoptive admission is substantive evidence. Once adopted, the statement is treated as the party’s own.
topic: Opposing-party statements — FRE 801(d)(2)(B) · FRE 104(b)

q:
Correctional officer Fosse was beaten with a metal pipe and suffered a fractured skull. Three weeks later, from his hospital bed, he told FBI Agent Lund that inmate Corley attacked him and picked Corley’s photograph from an array.

At Corley’s trial, Fosse testifies that he clearly remembers identifying Corley to Agent Lund in the hospital, but that because of his head injury he now has no memory of seeing his attacker and cannot explain the basis for his identification. The prosecution then calls Agent Lund to recount Fosse’s identification. Corley objects on hearsay and Confrontation Clause grounds.

How should the court rule?
o: Admit Lund’s testimony, because Fosse testified and was subject to cross-examination about his prior identification, even though he cannot recall its basis.
Exclude Lund’s testimony, because Fosse’s memory loss makes him “unavailable,” and an unavailable declarant cannot be “subject to cross-examination.”
Exclude Lund’s testimony, because an identification made three weeks after the event is too remote in time.
Admit Lund’s testimony only to impeach Fosse’s testimony that he cannot remember his attacker.
Exclude Lund’s testimony, because Fosse’s identification was made to a law-enforcement officer and is therefore testimonial.
e: Rule: A testifying declarant’s prior statement identifying a person as someone the declarant perceived earlier is not hearsay if the declarant is subject to cross-examination about it. FRE 801(d)(1)(C). The Confrontation Clause and the rule are satisfied when the witness takes the stand and answers questions, even if memory loss limits the answers. United States v. Owens.
oe: Correct. This is Owens: a witness who takes the stand and answers questions is subject to cross-examination, even with memory loss.
Owens rejected this argument. Memory loss can be unavailability for Rule 804 purposes while the witness remains subject to cross for Rule 801(d)(1).
Rule 801(d)(1)(C) has no time limit. Delay goes to weight.
The identification is substantive evidence under 801(d)(1)(C), not merely impeachment.
The identification is testimonial, but the Clause is satisfied because Fosse appears at trial and is subject to cross-examination.
topic: Prior statements & impeachment — FRE 801(d)(1)(C) · United States v. Owens

q:
Rennick sues a delivery company for injuries suffered when one of its vans rear-ended her car. A month before trial, at her lawyer’s request, Rennick sees Dr. Abbas, an orthopedist retained only to evaluate her and testify. He will provide no treatment.

Rennick tells Dr. Abbas: “My lower back has had a shooting pain down my left leg ever since the delivery van slammed into me from behind. The driver was staring at his phone and never even braked.” At trial, Rennick offers Dr. Abbas’s testimony repeating her statement.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Exclude the entire statement, because statements to a physician consulted only for litigation are not covered by the medical-diagnosis exception.
Admit the description of her pain and that she was hit from behind by a van, but exclude the statement that the driver was looking at his phone and never braked.
Admit the entire statement, because everything Rennick described concerned the cause of her injuries.
Admit only the description of her present pain, because statements about past symptoms and medical history are excluded.
Exclude the entire statement, because Rennick is a party and may not offer her own out-of-court statements.
e: Rule: A statement made for, and reasonably pertinent to, medical diagnosis or treatment that describes medical history, past or present symptoms or sensations, their inception, or their general cause is admissible. FRE 803(4).
oe: The Federal Rules cover statements made for diagnosis alone, including to a doctor retained to testify.
Correct. General cause comes in; statements about fault do not.
General cause is covered; fault is not. The driver’s distraction is not pertinent to diagnosing a back injury.
The rule expressly covers medical history and past symptoms.
Rule 801(d)(2) is unavailable to Rennick for her own statement, but a party may offer her own statement under any applicable hearsay exception, including 803(4).
topic: 803: spontaneity, state of mind, medical — FRE 803(4) · Advisory Committee Note to FRE 803(4)

q:
Morrow is charged with being a felon in possession of a firearm. At trial, Officer Jett testifies on direct examination that during a traffic stop, Morrow told him (orally, not recorded): “Yeah, the gun’s mine. It’s in the glove box.”

Defense counsel immediately asks to elicit on cross the rest of what Morrow said in the same breath: “But I took it off my nephew an hour ago because he was talking about hurting himself, and I’m driving it to the police station right now.” The government objects that Morrow’s self-serving statement is inadmissible hearsay when offered by Morrow.

How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because Rule 106 applies only to writings and recorded statements.
Sustain the objection, because a party’s own statement escapes the hearsay rule only when offered by the opposing party, and no exception applies.
Overrule the objection, because once the government introduces part of a defendant’s statement, the defendant is automatically entitled to introduce the rest of it.
Sustain the objection for now, because Morrow may offer the remainder, if at all, only during his own case.

Overrule the objection if the court finds that fairness requires the remainder to correct a misleading impression created by the partial statement, because Rule 106 permits completion over a hearsay objection.
e: Rule: If a party introduces all or part of a statement, an adverse party may require the introduction, at that time, of any other part, or any other statement, that in fairness ought to be considered at the same time. The adverse party may do so over a hearsay objection. FRE 106 (as amended 2023).
oe: The 2023 amendment extended Rule 106 to oral statements.
This was the government’s winning argument in some circuits before 2023. The amended rule allows completion over a hearsay objection.
Completion is not automatic. The remainder must be needed in fairness, typically to correct a misleading impression.
Rule 106 allows completion at that time, during the government’s presentation. The point is that the jury hears the explanation while it hears the admission.
Correct. This states the fairness standard and the 2023 hearsay override.
topic: Residual, multiple hearsay, completeness — FRE 106 (2023 amendment) · FRE 801(d)(2)(A)

q:
Sutter is charged with a bank robbery committed by a lone gunman with a sawed-off shotgun. Sutter calls Rhee, who shared a jail cell last year with Kirby, now deceased. Rhee will testify that Kirby told him: “I’m the one who did the Elm Street bank job. Used the sawed-off I keep under my mattress.”

A sawed-off shotgun was found under Kirby’s mattress after his death. But Kirby was a notorious jailhouse braggart who regularly claimed credit for high-profile crimes to build status, and a bank surveillance image shows that the robber was several inches taller than Kirby. The government objects.

Under the current version of Rule 804(b)(3), how should the court evaluate Kirby’s statement?
o: Admit it, because the corroboration requirement applies only to statements offered by the prosecution against the accused.
Admit it, because Kirby is unavailable and his statement exposed him to criminal liability; corroboration goes only to weight.

Consider only the circumstances in which Kirby made the statement, such as his bragging habit, and disregard the shotgun and surveillance evidence, which bear on the statement’s truth rather than its trustworthiness.

Admit it only if corroborating circumstances clearly indicate its trustworthiness, considering both the circumstances under which Kirby made it and any evidence, such as the shotgun and the surveillance image, that supports or undermines it.
Exclude it, because statements to cellmates are never against interest, since inmates commonly boast to each other without fear of prosecution.
e: Rule: A statement against penal interest offered in a criminal case must be “supported by corroborating circumstances that clearly indicate its trustworthiness, after considering the totality of circumstances under which it was made and any evidence that supports or undermines it.” FRE 804(b)(3)(B) (as amended 2024).
oe: Since 2010, corroboration is required for statements against penal interest offered by either side in a criminal case.
Corroboration is an admissibility requirement decided by the judge, not merely a matter of weight.
This was one side of the pre-2024 split. The amended rule requires considering independent evidence that supports or undermines the statement.
Correct. This tracks the 2024 text of Rule 804(b)(3)(B).
There is no categorical rule. Whether a reasonable person would make the statement only if true is a fact-specific question; a boasting context bears on it but does not settle it.
topic: 804: declarant unavailable — FRE 804(b)(3) (2024 amendment) · FRE 104(a)

q:
Lorna slipped on spilled soda in aisle 7 of a grocery store and sued the store for negligence. The store contends there was no spill at all and that Lorna tripped over her own feet.
