At trial, Lorna calls a cashier, who testifies that about 40 minutes before the fall, a shopper she did not know walked up to the store manager and said: “Somebody dropped a big bottle of soda in aisle 7. It’s all over the floor.” The shopper had passed through aisle 7 roughly twenty minutes before she said it. The store objects.

What is the proper ruling?
o: Admit the statement for all purposes as a present sense impression.
Admit the statement for all purposes as an opposing-party statement, because the store’s manager heard it.
Admit the statement to show that the store had notice of a possible spill and, on request, instruct the jury not to consider it as proof that a spill actually existed.
Exclude the statement entirely, because notice matters only if there was a spill, so the statement’s relevance depends on its truth.
Exclude the statement, because the shopper is unidentified and her personal knowledge cannot be shown.
e: Rule: A statement offered to show its effect on the listener, such as notice, knowledge, or a reason for later action, is not offered for its truth and is not hearsay for that purpose. The court must, on timely request, restrict the evidence to its proper purpose and instruct the jury accordingly. FRE 105.
oe: A twenty-minute gap is too long for “while or immediately after perceiving.”
The shopper was not the store’s agent, and nothing shows the manager adopted the statement.
Correct. The statement is admissible for notice, with a limiting instruction on request.
Notice is a separate element from the existence of the hazard. A warning is relevant to what the store knew regardless of its truth; Lorna must prove the spill with other evidence.
When a statement is offered only for its effect on the listener, the declarant’s knowledge is irrelevant.
topic: Definition & non-truth uses — FRE 801(c) · FRE 105

q:
J.T., a three-year-old, arrives at preschool with a bloodshot eye and red marks on his face. His teacher asks, “Who did this? What happened?” J.T. answers, “Jax did.” The teachers, who are required by state law to report suspected child abuse, call a hotline. Jax, the mother’s boyfriend, is charged with child abuse.

The court finds J.T. incompetent to testify. The prosecution offers the teacher’s testimony repeating J.T.’s statement, and Jax objects under the Confrontation Clause.

Which is the most accurate analysis?
o: The statement is not testimonial, because its primary purpose was to protect a young child from ongoing abuse, the exchange was informal, very young children rarely understand the prosecutorial use of their words, and teachers are not law enforcement officers even when they have a duty to report.
The statement is testimonial, because mandatory-reporting laws make teachers agents of law enforcement for Confrontation Clause purposes.
The statement is testimonial, because the teacher’s question, “Who did this?”, was directed at identifying a perpetrator.
The statement is admissible under the Confrontation Clause because it bears sufficient indicia of reliability.
The Confrontation Clause does not apply, because J.T. is incompetent and therefore could never have been a “witness” against Jax.
e: Rule: Statements to persons other than law enforcement officers are much less likely to be testimonial. A statement is testimonial only if, in light of all the circumstances, its primary purpose was to create an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony. Ohio v. Clark.
oe: Correct. This is the reasoning of Ohio v. Clark.
Clark expressly rejected the argument that mandatory-reporting duties make teachers agents of law enforcement.
Asking who caused the injuries is consistent with an emergency purpose: the teachers needed to know whether the child was safe to send home.
Reliability is the overruled Ohio v. Roberts test. For nontestimonial statements, the Clause simply does not apply; for testimonial ones, reliability is not enough.
Competence to testify is not the test. The question is the primary purpose of the statement, and the analysis would be the same for an older child.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — Ohio v. Clark · Crawford v. Washington

q:
At Veltri’s trial for securities fraud, the court admits, as a co-conspirator statement, an email from Pask to another conspirator: “Veltri signed off on the fake revenue numbers.” Pask does not testify.

Veltri then offers (1) a certified record of Pask’s wire-fraud conviction from four years ago and (2) testimony from Pask’s former assistant that, a month after the email, Pask told her, “Veltri never knew about the revenue numbers.” Pask was never asked about this later statement because he never testified. The prosecution objects to both.

How should the court rule?
o: Exclude both, because Rule 806 applies only to hearsay, and a co-conspirator statement is by definition not hearsay.
Admit the conviction, but exclude the later statement, because Pask was never given an opportunity to explain or deny it.
Exclude the conviction, because a non-testifying declarant’s credibility may be attacked only with evidence of inconsistent statements.
Admit the later statement as substantive evidence that Veltri lacked knowledge, but exclude the conviction as unfairly prejudicial.
Admit both to attack Pask’s credibility, even though Pask had no opportunity to explain or deny the inconsistent statement.
e: Rule: When a hearsay statement, or a statement described in Rule 801(d)(2)(C), (D), or (E), has been admitted, the declarant’s credibility may be attacked by any evidence that would be admissible if the declarant had testified. The court may admit evidence of the declarant’s inconsistent statement or conduct regardless of when it occurred or whether the declarant had an opportunity to explain or deny it. FRE 806.
oe: Rule 806 expressly applies to statements under 801(d)(2)(C), (D), and (E).
Rule 806 dispenses with the opportunity to explain or deny, because the declarant is not on the stand.
Any impeachment that would be proper against a live witness is proper against the declarant, including convictions under Rule 609.
The later statement is impeachment, not substantive evidence, unless an exception applies. The wire-fraud conviction is automatically admissible under Rule 609(a)(2), with no balancing.
Correct. Rule 806 allows both forms of impeachment and waives the foundation requirement.
topic: Prior statements & impeachment — FRE 806 · FRE 609(a)(2)

q:
Holt is prosecuted for setting fire to his own warehouse. The state fire marshal’s office, an agency authorized by statute to investigate fires, issued a report concluding after investigation that the fire “was most likely accidental, caused by faulty wiring in the east wall.” The same report records the observation of a police detective who toured the scene: “strong odor of gasoline near the loading door.”

Consider two offers:
(I) Holt offers the marshal’s conclusion that the fire was most likely accidental.
(II) The prosecution offers the detective’s observation of a gasoline odor, as recorded in the report, without calling the detective.

Which is admissible under Rule 803(8)?
o: Both I and II.
I only.
II only.
Neither, because Rule 803(8) applies only in civil cases.
Neither, because opinions and conclusions in public reports are never admissible.
e: Rule: A public record setting out factual findings from a legally authorized investigation is admissible in a civil case or against the government in a criminal case. FRE 803(8)(A)(iii). Matters observed by law-enforcement personnel are excluded in criminal cases. FRE 803(8)(A)(ii). In either case, the opponent may show that the source of information or other circumstances indicate a lack of trustworthiness. FRE 803(8)(B).
oe: The police observation is excluded in a criminal case under 803(8)(A)(ii).
Correct. Findings may be used against the government in a criminal case; police observations may not be used by the prosecution.
This reverses the rule’s asymmetry.
Rule 803(8) applies in criminal cases, subject to the law-enforcement exclusion and the against-the-government limit on findings.
Beech Aircraft held that conclusions and opinions based on a factual investigation are within “factual findings.”
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 803(8)(A)(ii)–(iii) · Beech Aircraft Corp. v. Rainey

q:
Detective Arno, testifying for the prosecution in a burglary case, cannot recall the serial number of a laptop recovered from the defendant’s car. The prosecutor hands Arno a page from another detective’s notes, which Arno did not write and has never adopted. Arno reads it silently, hands it back, and testifies that his memory is refreshed and that the serial number was “C02XK4471.” Defense counsel objects.

Which statement is correct?
o: The testimony must be stricken, because a witness’s memory may be refreshed only with a writing the witness personally prepared.
The testimony must be stricken, because the notes are hearsay and satisfy no exception.
The prosecutor may now offer the notes into evidence as substantive proof of the serial number, because they refreshed Arno’s memory.
The defense is entitled to have the notes produced, to inspect them, to cross-examine Arno about them, and to introduce in evidence any portion that relates to Arno’s testimony.
The defense is entitled to inspect the notes only if the court, in its discretion, finds that justice requires it.
e: Rule: If a witness uses a writing to refresh memory while testifying, an adverse party is entitled to have the writing produced at the hearing, to inspect it, to cross-examine the witness about it, and to introduce in evidence any portion that relates to the witness’s testimony. If the writing was used before testifying, those rights exist only if the court decides that justice requires it. FRE 612.
oe: Any writing, or anything else, may be used to refresh memory. Authorship matters for recorded recollection under 803(5), not for refreshing.
The notes are not offered as evidence, so the hearsay rule does not apply. The testimony is Arno’s refreshed memory.
Refreshing does not make the writing admissible for the proponent. The prosecution would need an independent basis, such as 803(5) or 803(6).
Correct. These are the adverse party’s rights under Rule 612(b) for a writing used while testifying.
The “justice requires” discretion applies only to writings used before testifying, under 612(a)(2).
topic: 803: records & recollection — FRE 612 · FRE 803(5)

q:
Ash and Bly are tried jointly for robbing a pharmacy. After his arrest, Ash gave police a written confession: “Bly and I planned it for a week. Bly had the gun; I drove.” Neither defendant will testify. Other evidence, including surveillance footage of a getaway car and phone records, connects Bly to Ash on the day of the robbery. The prosecution proposes to introduce Ash’s confession.

Which proposal is most likely constitutional as to Bly?
o: Introduce the confession unredacted, with an instruction that the jury may consider it only against Ash.
Introduce the confession with Bly’s name replaced by a blank space or the word “deleted,” with a limiting instruction.

Introduce the confession redacted to read, “The other guy and I planned it for a week. The other guy had the gun; I drove,” with a limiting instruction, even though other evidence may lead the jury to infer that “the other guy” is Bly.
Introduce the confession unredacted, because Ash’s confession interlocks with a confession that Bly also gave.
Introduce the confession unredacted against both defendants, because each defendant’s confession is an opposing-party statement.
e: Rule: At a joint trial, admitting a non-testifying co-defendant’s confession that facially incriminates the defendant violates the Confrontation Clause, even with a limiting instruction. Bruton v. United States. A confession redacted to eliminate any reference to the defendant may be admitted with a limiting instruction (Richardson v. Marsh), but obvious redactions such as blanks or “deleted” are treated like unredacted confessions (Gray v. Maryland). A neutral substitute such as “the other person,” with a limiting instruction, is permissible even if other evidence links it to the defendant. Samia v. United States (2023).
oe: Bruton held that a limiting instruction cannot cure a facially incriminating confession by a non-testifying co-defendant.
Gray v. Maryland treats obvious deletions as equivalent to naming the defendant.
Correct. This is the neutral-substitution redaction approved in Samia.
The Supreme Court has rejected an interlocking-confession exception: a codefendant’s confession that names the defendant is not cured by the defendant’s own similar confession.
Ash’s confession is an opposing-party statement only against Ash. Rule 801(d)(2)(A) does not make it admissible against Bly.
topic: Confrontation & Bruton — Bruton v. United States · Richardson v. Marsh

q:
Kade is charged with murdering a convenience-store clerk. The night of the killing, Kade’s girlfriend, Joss, texted her sister: “Kade just came home and told me he shot the clerk at the Gas-N-Go. I’m so scared.” Joss died in an unrelated car accident before trial.

The prosecution offers the sister’s testimony and a properly authenticated screenshot of the text.

What is Kade’s strongest argument for exclusion?
o: Joss’s text is hearsay, and her layer needs its own exception: Kade’s statement to her is an opposing-party statement, but Joss’s report of it must independently fit an exception.
Admitting the text violates the Confrontation Clause, because Joss is unavailable and Kade never had an opportunity to cross-examine her.
Kade’s statement to Joss is inadmissible hearsay, because it was not made under oath.
The text is inadmissible because a screenshot is not the original writing.
Joss’s statement is inadmissible, because a statement against penal interest must be made to law enforcement.
e: Rule: Hearsay within hearsay is admissible only if each layer conforms with an exception or exclusion. FRE 805. The Confrontation Clause applies only to testimonial statements; nontestimonial hearsay is governed by the rules of evidence alone. Crawford; Davis; Whorton v. Bockting.
oe: Correct. Rule 805 requires an exception for Joss’s layer, and that is where the real dispute lies.
A casual text to a sister is not testimonial, so the Confrontation Clause does not apply.
A party’s own statements are not hearsay under 801(d)(2)(A) and need no oath.
A screenshot of electronically stored information is an “original” or at least a “duplicate” under Rules 1001 and 1003.
Rule 804(b)(3) has no requirement that the statement be made to police. And Joss’s statement does not inculpate Joss in any event.
topic: Residual, multiple hearsay, completeness — FRE 805 · FRE 801(d)(2)(A)
